title: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
scopeHtml:
Scope: headers, methods, caching headers, cookies, CORS, keep-alive, head-of-line blocking across versions.

Scope: headers, methods, caching headers, cookies, CORS, keep-alive, head-of-line blocking across versions.

notes.title: HTTP basics: requests, responses, methods
notes.html:
HTTP is a request/response protocol: the client sends a method, a path, headers and an optional body; the server replies with a status code, headers and a body. It is stateless: each request stands alone.

GET /orders/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.shop.com
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 58
Method Meaning Safe Idempotent
GET Read yes yes
HEAD Headers only yes yes
POST Create/action no no
PUT Replace no yes
PATCH Partial update no not guaranteed
DELETE Remove no yes
OPTIONS What is allowed (CORS preflight) yes yes

Status families. 2xx ok (200, 201, 204), 3xx redirect (301 permanent, 302/307 temporary, 304 not modified), 4xx client error (400, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404, 409 conflict, 429 rate limit), 5xx server (500, 502 bad gateway, 503 unavailable, 504 gateway timeout).

Worked example. Idempotency matters for retries. A mobile app times out on POST /payments. Retrying may charge twice. Stripe solves it with an Idempotency-Key header: the server stores the first result for that key (24 h) and returns it for repeats. PUT /users/7 can be retried blindly.

Industry examples. REST APIs at Stripe, GitHub and Twilio follow these methods and use 429 plus Retry-After. 502 vs 504 is the daily vocabulary of ops: 502 means the proxy got garbage or a closed connection, 504 means it waited too long.

Everyday analogy. Posting a letter and getting a reply: the method is what you ask ("tell me", "store this"), the status is the first line of the answer ("done", "not here", "we messed up").

Common interview traps.

  • Calling POST idempotent, or using GET for actions that change state (crawlers and prefetch will trigger them).
  • Confusing 401 (who are you?) with 403 (I know you, no).
  • Returning 200 with an error in the body; breaks caches, monitors and retries.

notes.title: HTTP/1.1: keep-alive and its limits
notes.html:
HTTP/1.1 reuses one TCP connection for many requests (keep-alive, default since 1.1), but responses must come back in order on that connection.

Without keep-alive every request pays TCP handshake (1 RTT) plus TLS (1 to 2 RTT). With a 100 ms RTT that is 200 to 300 ms before the first byte. Keep-alive removes that for later requests.

The limit is head-of-line (HOL) blocking at the HTTP level: request 2 cannot be answered until response 1 is finished. Pipelining (sending several without waiting) existed but was broken in practice and is disabled in browsers. Workarounds browsers used: open 6 parallel connections per host, and sites used domain sharding, sprite sheets and bundling to cut requests.

Worked example. A page needs 60 assets. With 6 connections and 100 ms per request round, the minimum is 60/6 x 100 ms = 1 s of pure waiting, even on a fast link. Bundling to 10 files cuts it to about 200 ms.

Config (nginx).

# nginx.conf (keepalive to clients and upstreams)
keepalive_timeout 65;
keepalive_requests 1000;
upstream api { server 10.0.0.5:8080; keepalive 64; }
# proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Connection "";

Industry examples. HTTP/1.1 is still what many internal services and simple clients speak. A slow upstream behind a proxy with keepalive off causes connection churn (TIME_WAIT pile-ups, ephemeral port exhaustion).

Everyday analogy. A single-lane drive-through: you can keep the lane open for many cars, but a slow order delays everyone behind it.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying pipelining solves HOL blocking in 1.1 (it does not, in practice).
  • Forgetting that keepalive timeouts must be longer on the client side than on the server, or a race closes a connection mid-request (classic sporadic 502 behind AWS ALB when the app idle timeout is shorter than the ALB's 60 s).

notes.title: HTTP/2: multiplexing
notes.html:
HTTP/2 sends many requests as interleaved binary frames over ONE TCP connection, so a slow response no longer blocks others at the HTTP layer.

Key features:

  • Streams and frames: each request/response is a numbered stream; frames from different streams interleave.
  • HPACK header compression: repeated headers (cookies, user-agent) cost a few bytes after the first request. Saves 80 to 90% of header bytes.
  • Stream prioritization and flow control per stream and per connection.
  • Server push: sent assets before asked. Largely abandoned; Chrome removed it.
  • Usually requires TLS in browsers (ALPN negotiates h2).
Stream 1: HEADERS(GET /a) ....... DATA DATA
Stream 3: HEADERS(GET /b) .. DATA ..... DATA
Stream 5: HEADERS(GET /c) DATA
(all in one TCP connection, interleaved)

Worked example. The 60-asset page: one connection, all 60 requests started at once. Time is about 1 RTT plus transfer time instead of 10 sequential rounds. Bundling and sharding become anti-patterns (sharding even hurts, since it kills multiplexing).

The catch: TCP HOL blocking. All streams share one TCP byte stream. If one packet is lost, TCP holds back everything after it until retransmit. On lossy mobile networks (2% loss) HTTP/2 can be slower than six HTTP/1.1 connections.

Industry examples. gRPC runs on HTTP/2. Nginx, Envoy, Cloudflare, AWS ALB all speak it. Google created SPDY, the ancestor.

Decision gravity. Enabling h2 at the edge is reversible and safe (clients fall back). Keep h2 for client-to-edge, and consider HTTP/1.1 or h2 to origin depending on proxy support.

Everyday analogy. A single conveyor belt carrying mixed packages for many customers, rather than one belt per customer. If the belt jams, every customer waits.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing HTTP/2 removes all head-of-line blocking; TCP-level HOL remains.
  • Claiming h2 is faster for one big file; it is not.
  • Forgetting max concurrent streams (often 100 to 128) and HTTP/2 rapid reset attacks (2023), which led to server hardening.

notes.title: HTTP/3 and QUIC
notes.html:
HTTP/3 runs HTTP over QUIC, a transport built on UDP, so lost packets only stall the one stream they belong to.

QUIC features:

  • Per-stream loss recovery: removes TCP HOL blocking.
  • TLS 1.3 built in: handshake in 1 RTT, and 0-RTT for repeat visits (replayable, so only for safe requests).
  • Connection IDs: a connection survives a switch from Wi-Fi to cellular (connection migration), because it is not tied to the IP/port 4-tuple.
  • User-space implementation: easier to evolve than kernel TCP; but more CPU.
  • Discovered by the Alt-Svc: h3=":443" header or HTTPS DNS record; browsers fall back to h2 if UDP 443 is blocked.

Worked example. RTT 80 ms to a mobile user. HTTP/2 with TLS 1.3: 1 RTT TCP + 1 RTT TLS + 1 request = ~240 ms to first byte. HTTP/3: 1 RTT handshake + request = ~160 ms; with 0-RTT resumption ~80 ms.

Industry examples. Google, YouTube, Facebook, Cloudflare and Netflix use HTTP/3; roughly a quarter to a third of web traffic by 2024. Corporate firewalls that drop UDP are the main blocker.

Decision gravity. Enabling h3 at a CDN is a toggle (reversible). Self-hosting needs UDP load balancing (QUIC connection-ID-aware, e.g. Katran) and watching CPU, a bigger commitment.

Everyday analogy. Separate lanes in a motorway that do not stop when one lane has a crash, and a car that keeps its toll tag even when it takes a different road.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying QUIC is "UDP so unreliable". Reliability is implemented in QUIC.
  • Forgetting UDP may be blocked or rate-limited: always keep h2 fallback.
  • 0-RTT replay risk for non-idempotent requests.

notes.title: Headers that matter
notes.html:
Headers are key-value metadata. The ones used in nearly every incident:

  • Host: which site on this IP (required in 1.1; :authority in h2/h3).
  • Content-Type / Accept / Content-Length / Transfer-Encoding: chunked: body description. Request smuggling arises when proxies disagree about Content-Length vs chunked.
  • Authorization: Bearer <token> or Basic.
  • User-Agent, Accept-Encoding (gzip, br), Content-Encoding: compression cuts JSON by 70 to 90%.
  • X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, Forwarded: the real client IP and scheme once a proxy is in the path. Trust only the proxy-appended last hop.
  • Location: redirect target.
  • Retry-After: how long to wait on 429/503.
  • Connection / Upgrade: protocol switch (WebSocket).
  • Cache-Control, ETag, Vary: next section.

Tool sample.

$ curl -sI https://api.shop.com/orders/42
HTTP/2 200
content-type: application/json
cache-control: private, max-age=0
etag: "a1b2c3"
content-encoding: br
x-request-id: 7f3e...

Worked example. A 200 KB JSON response compresses to ~30 KB with gzip. At 1,000 rps that is 1,000 x 170 KB = 170 MB/s of bandwidth saved, ~1.4 Gbit/s.

Everyday analogy. The labels on a parcel: where from, what is inside, handle with care, return address.

Common interview traps.

  • Trusting X-Forwarded-For from the client for rate limiting or auth: it can be forged.
  • Forgetting Vary: Accept-Encoding (cache serves gzip to a client that cannot read it).
  • Header size limits (8 KB in nginx by default) breaking large cookies with 431/400 errors.

notes.title: Caching headers
notes.html:
HTTP caching lets browsers, CDNs and proxies reuse a response instead of asking the origin again. Two mechanisms: freshness (do not even ask) and validation (ask cheaply "has it changed?").

  • Cache-Control: max-age=3600 (browser), s-maxage=86400 (shared caches such as CDN), public, private (browser only), no-store (never keep), no-cache (keep but revalidate), immutable, stale-while-revalidate=60.
  • Validators: ETag: "v7" with request If-None-Match: "v7"; or Last-Modified with If-Modified-Since. If unchanged, the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body.
  • Vary: which request headers change the response (e.g. Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language).
1st:  GET /app.js            -> 200, ETag "v7", max-age=60, 300 KB
2nd (after 60 s):
      GET /app.js If-None-Match "v7" -> 304, 0 KB body

Worked example (best practice). Fingerprinted assets app.4f9a2c.js: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. HTML: Cache-Control: no-cache so it always revalidates but is cheap via ETag. API with user data: private, no-store. A CDN hit ratio of 95% on 10,000 rps means the origin sees 500 rps instead of 10,000.

Industry examples. Cloudflare, Fastly and CloudFront honour s-maxage; GitHub serves releases with long cache and ETags. Fastly pioneered fast purge.

Decision gravity. A long max-age on a non-fingerprinted URL is nearly a one-way door: you cannot recall copies in users' browsers. Prefer versioned URLs.

Everyday analogy. Keeping yesterday's newspaper: still fresh if the news cannot have changed; otherwise phone the paper and ask "anything new?"; they say "no" in two words (304).

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing no-cache (revalidate) with no-store (do not store).
  • Caching personalised responses publicly (a classic data leak: one user's page served to another).
  • Forgetting Vary or cookies, so the CDN fragment cache explodes or leaks.

notes.title: Cookies and sessions
notes.html:
A cookie is a small value the server asks the browser to store and send back on every request to that site. It is how a stateless protocol gets "login".

Set-Cookie: sid=abc123; Path=/; Max-Age=1800; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

  • Secure: only over HTTPS.
  • HttpOnly: JavaScript cannot read it (blunts XSS theft).
  • SameSite: Strict, Lax (default in modern browsers), None (needs Secure) controls sending on cross-site requests (CSRF defence).
  • Domain/Path/Max-Age/Expires: scope and lifetime.
  • Limit about 4 KB each, ~50 per domain; sent with every request, so large cookies waste bandwidth (and defeat CDN caching).
  • __Host- prefix forces Secure, no Domain, Path=/.

Worked example. A 2 KB cookie on 40 requests per page load = 80 KB upstream per page, on a slow mobile uplink (1 Mbit/s) about 0.6 s. Serve static assets from a cookieless domain, or keep the cookie small and put data in the server-side session store.

Industry examples. Chrome phasing out third-party cookies and defaulting to SameSite=Lax changed how embedded widgets, SSO and ad tech work. Mobile apps typically use bearer tokens instead.

Everyday analogy. A wristband at a concert: shown at every gate, and it says which ticket you hold, not who you are.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing the session data in the cookie unsigned.
  • Missing Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite on auth cookies.
  • Forgetting cookies are per-domain and the sub-domain (Domain=) scoping rules.

notes.title: CORS
notes.html:
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the browser's rule that a page from one origin may only read responses from another origin if that server explicitly allows it. An origin is scheme + host + port. It is enforced by browsers, not servers; curl ignores it.

Flow:

  • Simple request (GET, simple POST with basic headers): browser sends it with an Origin header; response must include Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
  • Preflight: for PUT/DELETE, JSON content type or custom headers (Authorization), browser first sends OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method/Headers; server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, Access-Control-Max-Age (cache the preflight, e.g. 600).
  • Credentials: cookies cross-origin need Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and a specific origin (not *).

Config (nginx).

# add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin "https://app.shop.com" always;
# add_header Access-Control-Allow-Methods "GET, POST, OPTIONS" always;
# add_header Access-Control-Allow-Headers "Authorization, Content-Type" always;
# add_header Access-Control-Max-Age 600 always;
# add_header Vary Origin always;

Worked example. SPA at app.shop.com calls api.shop.com with an Authorization header: each call is two requests (OPTIONS + GET). With Max-Age: 600 the preflight is cached 10 minutes, cutting API traffic by ~half.

Industry examples. Public APIs like GitHub's allow * for unauthenticated reads. Many "CORS errors" in the console are really a 500/502 that lacks CORS headers, hiding the real error.

Everyday analogy. A building where residents may only read mail from another floor if that floor's concierge has pre-approved them.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking CORS is server-side security. It protects users' browsers, not your API.
  • Allow-Origin: * with credentials is rejected.
  • Reflecting any Origin header back: effectively disables the protection. Also forgetting Vary: Origin when allow-listing.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• HTTP is stateless request/response: methods (safe/idempotent), status families, headers; use idempotency keys for payments.
  • HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reuses a connection but suffers HTTP-level head-of-line blocking; browsers open about 6 connections.
  • HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection with HPACK; TCP-level HOL blocking remains on loss.
  • HTTP/3 over QUIC (UDP) fixes that, has 1-RTT/0-RTT setup and connection migration; keep h2 fallback.
  • Caching: Cache-Control, ETag/304, Vary; fingerprint static assets and give them a year, never cache private data publicly.
  • Cookies need Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite; keep them small.
  • CORS is a browser rule enforced via Origin and preflight OPTIONS; cache preflights; never reflect arbitrary origins.

questions.promptHtml: What do "safe" and "idempotent" mean for HTTP methods, and why does it matter for retries?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Retry and caching correctness depends on it; common source of double charges.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Safe means no state change (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS). Idempotent means repeating gives the same server state as doing it once (GET, PUT, DELETE, plus the safe ones). POST is neither, PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent. Proxies and clients may retry idempotent requests automatically, so a non-idempotent POST needs an idempotency key.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
If a connection drops after the request is sent but before the response arrives, the client cannot know whether the server processed it. For idempotent methods a retry is safe; for POST it may create a duplicate. Idempotent does not mean same response: DELETE returns 204 first, 404 afterwards, but the state is the same. Caches only store responses to GET/HEAD by default.

Method Safe Idempotent
GET/HEAD yes yes
PUT/DELETE no yes
POST no no
PATCH no no (depends)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/payments \
  -H 'Idempotency-Key: 7f3c-91ab' -d '{"amount":100}'

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using GET for actions (crawlers and prefetchers trigger them).
  • Assuming PUT is non-idempotent because it writes.
  • Auto-retrying POST in a client library without keys.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you make POST safe to retry? -> Idempotency key stored with the result server-side.
  2. What status for a duplicate key? -> Return the original response.
  3. Is DELETE returning 404 on retry a violation? -> No; state, not response, is what idempotent means.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists method meanings. Senior links to retry policy, load balancer behavior and idempotency-key storage.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mobile client retried a timed-out POST /orders three times, creating duplicate orders until an idempotency key was added.

questions.promptHtml: Explain Cache-Control, ETag and conditional requests. How is no-cache different from no-store?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The names are misleading; wrong settings leak data or kill performance.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: max-age says how long a response is fresh. After that the cache revalidates using If-None-Match (ETag) or If-Modified-Since, and the server answers 304 with no body if unchanged. no-cache means "store it but revalidate before use"; no-store means "never store it". private restricts to the browser; public allows shared caches.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A response is fresh until age exceeds max-age (or s-maxage for shared caches). Stale responses can still be reused if revalidation returns 304. immutable tells browsers not to revalidate fingerprinted assets. stale-while-revalidate serves stale while refreshing in background. Vary declares which request headers form part of the cache key (e.g. Vary: Accept-Encoding).

GET /app.js            -> 200, ETag: "abc", Cache-Control: max-age=300
(after 300 s) GET + If-None-Match: "abc" -> 304 Not Modified

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using no-cache thinking it disables caching of sensitive data (use no-store).
  • Caching HTML with long max-age but no versioned URLs.
  • Missing Vary so a CDN serves the wrong variant.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is cache busting? -> Fingerprint in filename (app.3fa2.js) with long immutable max-age.
  2. Strong vs weak ETag? -> Byte-identical vs semantically same.
  3. What does s-maxage do? -> Overrides max-age for shared caches (CDN).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average says "caches for X seconds". Senior designs by asset type: immutable fingerprinted assets, short HTML TTL with revalidation, private for personalised responses.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A CDN cached a personalised API response because Cache-Control: private was missing and users saw others' data.

questions.promptHtml: What does HTTP keep-alive solve and what limits remain in HTTP/1.1?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Foundation for why HTTP/2 exists.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep-alive reuses a TCP (and TLS) connection for multiple requests, avoiding repeated handshakes and slow-start restarts. But HTTP/1.1 still handles one request at a time per connection: responses must come back in order, so a slow response blocks the ones behind it. Browsers work around this with about 6 parallel connections per host.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Each new connection costs a TCP handshake (1 RTT), TLS (1-2 RTT) and starts with a small congestion window. Reuse removes this. HTTP/1.1 pipelining (several requests without waiting) was specified but is effectively dead because of HoL blocking and proxy bugs. Domain sharding was a hack to get more parallel connections. Idle timeouts matter: if the server closes an idle connection at the same moment the client reuses it, the client gets a reset on a "good" connection.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Client idle timeout longer than server/LB idle timeout, causing random resets.
  • Too many connections per client overwhelming the server.
  • Believing pipelining is widely used.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why 6 connections? -> Browser convention to balance parallelism and server load.
  2. What's HoL blocking at HTTP level? -> Response order is fixed, so a slow one blocks the rest.
  3. How do you avoid keep-alive races? -> Client idle timeout less than server's; retry idempotent requests.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "reuses connection". Senior adds idle-timeout mismatch, connection pooling sizing and why h2 changed the model.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Sporadic 502s from an ALB traced to backend closing idle connections at 60 s while the ALB kept them for 350 s.

questions.promptHtml: How do HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 each deal with head-of-line blocking?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests precise understanding, since HTTP/2 only moved the problem.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: HTTP/1.1 blocks at the request level within a connection. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection, which fixes request-level blocking but one lost TCP segment still stalls all streams. HTTP/3 uses QUIC where streams are independent, so loss only blocks the affected stream.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
HTTP/2 frames from different streams interleave on one connection, with HPACK header compression and stream priorities. Because TCP delivers a single ordered byte stream, a gap blocks everything above it: at 2% loss, h2 over one connection can be worse than 6 parallel HTTP/1.1 connections. QUIC puts stream framing inside encrypted packets with per-stream ordering, so only streams with missing data wait. Note: inside a single stream, order is still preserved.

HTTP/1.1: [req1 resp1][req2 resp2]...      (per conn, serialized; 6 conns)
HTTP/2  : streams 1,3,5 interleaved on 1 TCP conn; one lost packet blocks all
HTTP/3  : streams 1,3,5 on QUIC; loss blocks only stream with the lost data

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying HTTP/2 eliminates HoL blocking.
  • Forgetting h2 needs one big connection; middleboxes timing out matters more.
  • Assuming h3 helps on low-loss, low-latency links.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When might h2 be slower than h1? -> High loss mobile links.
  2. Does h2 need TLS? -> Browsers only support it over TLS (ALPN h2).
  3. What replaced server push? -> It was removed from browsers; use 103 Early Hints/preload.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "h2 multiplexes". Senior: transport-level vs application-level HoL, loss sensitivity, and measures before migrating.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After enabling h2, a mobile-heavy site saw p99 regress in 4G dead zones until h3 was added.

questions.contextHtml:
A new SPA at https://app.example.com calls https://api.example.com/v1/orders with fetch(url, {method:'PUT', headers:{'Authorization':'Bearer ...','Content-Type':'application/json'}, credentials:'include'}). In the browser console: "blocked by CORS policy: Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check". But curl works fine, and Postman too. Backend dev says "I added Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *." Network tab:

OPTIONS /v1/orders  -> 403  (no CORS headers)

Red herring: API gateway logs show 200s for GETs.
questions.promptHtml: Why does it fail and what is the correct configuration?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disable CORS in the browser" or sets * and still fails with credentials.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the OPTIONS response contain? Is auth required on OPTIONS? Is a cookie or bearer used?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a handler that returns CORS headers for OPTIONS before auth.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The preflight is rejected by auth middleware (403); * is not allowed with credentials; missing Access-Control-Allow-Headers: authorization, content-type; method list lacks PUT; wrong origin string (port, scheme).
  4. How I'd verify each: curl -i -X OPTIONS -H 'Origin: https://app.example.com' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization,content-type' https://api.example.com/v1/orders.
  5. Root cause: PUT with custom headers triggers a preflight; the gateway runs auth first and rejects the unauthenticated OPTIONS, so no CORS headers appear. Also * cannot be used when credentials are included.
  6. Fix: Respond to OPTIONS with 204 and Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com, Allow-Methods: GET,PUT,POST, Allow-Headers: authorization,content-type, Allow-Credentials: true, Max-Age: 600, Vary: Origin.
  7. Prevention: Integration test that runs a real browser (Playwright) against staging; allow-list origins in config.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not reflect any Origin blindly with credentials (opens cross-site data theft); CORS is browser-only protection, not auth.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does curl work? -> CORS is enforced by browsers, not servers.
  • Same-site cookies? -> SameSite=None; Secure needed for cross-site cookies.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team "fixed" CORS by reflecting Origin with credentials, which let any site read user data; a security review caught it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: wildcard fiddling.
  • Hire: preflight reasoning and correct headers.
  • Strong hire: Vary, credentials rules, security implication, browser test.

questions.contextHtml:
After a release, some users see an old JavaScript bundle for days and the app breaks with API mismatch errors; a hard refresh fixes it. The CDN config and responses:

GET /index.html  -> 200  Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400
GET /static/main.js -> 200  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
Build output: static/main.js  (same filename every build)

CDN hit ratio is 98%. Red herring: the service worker was recently disabled.
questions.promptHtml: What's wrong and how do you fix it safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Clear the CDN cache" without fixing the design.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are filenames fingerprinted? Is HTML cached by CDN or browser? What is the rollback path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Purge /index.html and /static/main.js at the CDN; cannot reach browsers that cached immutable for a year, so ship a renamed bundle.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Non-fingerprinted file with immutable one-year cache; HTML cached 24 h pointing to old files; CDN tiered cache; service worker.
  4. How I'd verify each: curl -I both URLs; check Age and X-Cache; inspect network tab "from disk cache".
  5. Root cause: immutable plus one year on an unversioned filename means browsers never revalidate; HTML also cached for a day, so new HTML can't point to new asset names.
  6. Fix: Content-hash filenames (main.3fa21c.js) with immutable year-long caching; HTML with Cache-Control: no-cache (revalidate with ETag) or short max-age with stale-while-revalidate.
  7. Prevention: CI check that static assets have hashes; header tests; version endpoint to detect client mismatch.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not shorten asset TTL to fix it (loses cache benefits); keep old hashed assets for a while for clients with old HTML.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Users stuck with old main.js already? -> Change the HTML to load a new filename; those who cached HTML for 24 h converge within a day.
  • Can you target them? -> Use Clear-Site-Data header cautiously.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a one-year cache on app.js took a week of support tickets to recover from; versioned filenames ended the problem.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: purge only.
  • Hire: fingerprint plus HTML revalidation.
  • Strong hire: explains immutable consequences, old asset retention and monitoring.

questions.contextHtml:
You moved internal gRPC/HTTP2 traffic through a layer-4 NLB to a pool of 12 pods. Total 3k req/s via 8 client pods. After scaling the backend from 6 to 12 pods, the new pods receive almost no traffic, and two old pods run at 90% CPU. Connection counts:

pod-1: 8 conns  CPU 91%
pod-2: 8 conns  CPU 88%
pod-7: 0 conns  CPU 3%

Red herring: pod readiness is fine and the NLB reports all targets healthy.
questions.promptHtml: Why is load unbalanced and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "NLB algorithm is bad, switch to round-robin," without seeing connection-level balancing.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do clients keep long-lived connections? How many per client? Is there client-side load balancing?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart/rotate client pods or trigger reconnects so connections redistribute.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: L4 balancing happens per connection and h2 connections last forever; clients opened connections before new pods existed; DNS pinned; sticky settings.
  4. How I'd verify each: ss -tn state established | grep :8080 | wc -l per pod; client connection ages; NLB flow stats.
  5. Root cause: HTTP/2 multiplexes all requests on a few long-lived connections; the L4 balancer only chooses a backend at connect time, so scale-out doesn't redistribute.
  6. Fix: Use an L7 balancer (Envoy) that balances per request, or client-side load balancing with headless service / xDS; set MAX_CONNECTION_AGE (e.g. 5 min with grace) on servers so clients reconnect.
  7. Prevention: Alert on per-pod request skew; load test scale-out events.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Short connection ages add reconnect cost and brief errors without graceful GOAWAY; L7 adds a hop and cost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just more connections per client? -> Helps balance but increases memory; still not rebalancing on scale-out.
  • What is GOAWAY? -> h2 frame telling the client to stop new streams on this connection.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: autoscaling "didn't work" for weeks; the real cause was 8 long-lived gRPC channels pinned to the first 6 pods.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks LB algorithm.
  • Hire: identifies long-lived connections vs L4 balancing.
  • Strong hire: GOAWAY/max-age, L7 or client-side balancing, test.

questions.promptHtml: How do cookie attributes (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Domain) protect a session, and how do sessions work with cookies?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Session security basics and CSRF understanding.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The server sets a session ID in Set-Cookie; the browser returns it on each request, and the server looks up the session. HttpOnly hides it from JavaScript (limits XSS theft), Secure sends only over HTTPS, SameSite=Lax/Strict stops cross-site sends (limits CSRF), and Domain/Path scope where it goes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
HTTP is stateless; cookies add state. A session cookie holds an opaque ID (server-side session store, e.g. Redis) or a signed token (JWT) holding the data. SameSite=Lax (the modern browser default) sends cookies on top-level GET navigations but not cross-site POST/iframes; Strict never sends cross-site; None requires Secure. Prefix __Host- forces Secure, Path=/, and no Domain. Rotating the session ID on login prevents fixation. Cookie size limit is about 4 KB each and they are sent on every request, adding overhead.

Set-Cookie: sid=9f2...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=3600

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing tokens in localStorage, readable by any XSS.
  • SameSite=None without need.
  • Setting Domain to a parent domain, exposing the cookie to every subdomain (including takeover-prone ones).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does SameSite remove need for CSRF tokens? -> Reduces, not replaces, esp. for same-site attacks.
  2. Server-side session vs JWT? -> Revocation and size vs stateless scaling.
  3. What is session fixation? -> Attacker sets a known ID before login; rotate on auth.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists flags. Senior discusses CSRF, subdomain risk, rotation, revocation and cookie weight per request.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A login broke in an embedded iframe partner flow after browsers defaulted to SameSite=Lax; None; Secure was needed.

questions.promptHtml: Which request and response headers matter most in a production HTTP setup, and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests breadth of practical HTTP knowledge: proxies, security, compression.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Host (virtual hosting), Content-Type/Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding (framing), Accept-Encoding/Content-Encoding (compression), Authorization, X-Forwarded-For/Forwarded (client IP behind proxies), Cache-Control/ETag/Vary, Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, and Retry-After/429 for backoff.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Framing bugs (conflicting Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding) enable request smuggling between proxy and backend, so normalise at the edge. X-Forwarded-For is client-controlled: only trust entries appended by your own proxies, counting from the right. Vary: Accept-Encoding keeps gzip and brotli variants apart in caches. HSTS forces HTTPS for a period (preload list for permanence). CSP restricts script sources. Retry-After tells clients when to retry on 429/503. Content-Length is needed for keep-alive when not chunked.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.9, 10.0.0.4, 10.0.0.5   # leftmost can be spoofed
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Trusting the leftmost X-Forwarded-For for rate limiting or auth.
  • Missing Vary leading to cache poisoning.
  • Putting HSTS with includeSubDomains before all subdomains support HTTPS.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is request smuggling? -> Disagreement between front and back end on message boundaries.
  2. How do you get the real client IP? -> Trust only your proxies' appended entry, or use PROXY protocol.
  3. Why compress? -> Smaller transfers; careful with secrets (BREACH).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average names a few headers. Senior ties each to a failure mode: smuggling, spoofed IP, cache poisoning, HSTS lockout.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Rate limiting keyed on the leftmost XFF let one attacker bypass limits by rotating the header.

questions.contextHtml:
Behind an ALB (idle timeout 60 s) your Node.js service returns ~0.1% 502s at low traffic, mostly after quiet periods; at high traffic it is rare. Logs: ALB target_connection_error/502 ... backend closed connection. App is Node's default HTTP server. Red herring: CPU, memory and GC are fine.

Node: server.keepAliveTimeout = 5000 (default 5 s)
ALB idle timeout = 60 s
questions.promptHtml: Why do the 502s happen and how do you fix them?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale up" or add retries at the client.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are 502s correlated with idle gaps? Are POSTs affected? What are LB and server timeouts?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set Node keepAliveTimeout to above 60 s (e.g. 65 s) and headersTimeout above it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Server closes idle connection before the LB's idle timeout; LB reuses it at the same moment (race); app crashes; deployment draining.
  4. How I'd verify each: Correlate 502 with idle time; tcpdump shows FIN from the backend then LB sending a request, got RST; check target logs for the request (absent).
  5. Root cause: The backend's 5 s keep-alive timeout is shorter than the LB's 60 s. When the LB sends a request on a connection just closed by the backend, it gets a reset and returns 502.
  6. Fix: The upstream (server) keep-alive timeout must exceed the LB's idle timeout. Apply the same rule for any proxy chain.
  7. Prevention: Config standard: client < proxy < server idle timeouts; synthetic test with idle gaps of 4-6 s and 59-61 s.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Longer idle timeouts hold more sockets/file descriptors; don't rely on automatic retries for non-idempotent requests.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why more frequent at low traffic? -> Connections idle more often.
  • Does HTTP/2 fix it? -> Not by itself; idle connections still close; GOAWAY helps.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: months of 0.1% 502 "noise" vanished with a one-line timeout change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales up.
  • Hire: spots timeout mismatch.
  • Strong hire: ordering rule, reproduction test, idempotency caveat.

questions.contextHtml:
A CDN fronts your site. Security reports that https://shop.example.com/? sometimes returns a page whose links point to https://evil.example.net/. The origin builds absolute URLs from the X-Forwarded-Host header when present. CDN cache key: path + query only. Hit ratio 95%, TTL 10 min. A researcher shows one crafted request poisons the cache for all users for 10 minutes.

GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
X-Forwarded-Host: evil.example.net
questions.promptHtml: Explain the vulnerability, immediate response, and a durable fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sanitize the header" only, without addressing the cache key.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which unkeyed headers does the origin read? Does CDN forward unknown headers? Which pages affected?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Purge the cache; configure the CDN to strip X-Forwarded-Host (and similar) from client requests; temporarily disable caching for affected routes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Unkeyed header reflected into a cacheable response (web cache poisoning); Vary missing; other unkeyed headers (X-Forwarded-Scheme); host header injection.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay requests with and without header; use a cache buster query; Param Miner style header fuzzing; check origin code for header reads.
  5. Root cause: The origin response depends on an input (header) that is not part of the cache key, so an attacker's variant is stored and served to everyone.
  6. Fix: Origin must not trust client-supplied forwarding headers; build URLs from a configured canonical host; CDN overwrites forwarding headers at the edge; if variation is needed, add to cache key or Vary.
  7. Prevention: Tests for unkeyed inputs, security headers (CSP), regular cache-poisoning scans, log cache keys.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not just lower TTL (shorter window, still exploitable); adding headers to the key cuts hit ratio.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Related attack? -> Request smuggling and cache deception (caching private pages at static-looking paths).
  • Why is Vary: */Cookie a problem? -> Destroys hit ratio.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a poisoned home page served injected script for 8 minutes before purge; the origin trusted three forwarding headers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sanitizes header only.
  • Hire: explains unkeyed input and fixes at origin and edge.
  • Strong hire: cache-key design, scanning, related attacks.

questions.contextHtml: A news site (80% mobile, p75 RTT 120 ms, loss ~2% on 4G) wants to cut load time. Current: HTTP/2 over TLS 1.3, 90 requests per page, 1.8 MB, TTFB p75 480 ms. A vendor pitches HTTP/3 as "30% faster". Budget allows one quarter of work. RUM data shows 35% of sessions are repeat visits with TLS session resumption.
questions.promptHtml: Would you adopt HTTP/3, and what else would you do first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, enable HTTP/3, it's the future," with no measurement plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What dominates load: TTFB, third-party scripts, images? Which metrics matter (LCP)? CDN support?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; start with RUM segmentation.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Payload and third-party scripts dominate; h2 HoL on lossy mobile hurts; TTFB comes from origin/cache misses; handshake RTT matters on first visits.
  4. How I'd verify each: WebPageTest on throttled 4G with 2% loss comparing h2 vs h3; RUM split by nextHopProtocol; waterfall review.
  5. Root cause: Bytes and requests are the bigger lever; h3 helps mostly on lossy/high-RTT links (saves ~1 RTT of handshake and avoids HoL), less on stable ones.
  6. Fix: Plan: image optimization, critical CSS, defer third parties, cache tuning; enable h3 at the CDN as an A/B (alt-svc) with fallbacks and measure p75/p95 LCP by network type.
  7. Prevention: Performance budgets, RUM alerts by protocol and region.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not spend the quarter on custom QUIC; h3 raises server CPU and debugging difficulty; 0-RTT only for safe GETs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Gains on desktop fiber? -> Minimal.
  • Why alt-svc discovery means first visit uses h2? -> Client learns h3 after the first response (or HTTPS DNS record).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: h3 gave 5% on mobile p95 while removing a 600 KB tag manager gave 20%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adopts on hype.
  • Hire: proposes measurement and A/B.
  • Strong hire: compares levers, knows where h3 helps, accounts for cost and fallbacks.

questions.contextHtml: Your monolith uses in-memory sessions on 6 instances with sticky load balancing; deploys log users out and scale-out is uneven. Traffic: 20k concurrent sessions, 5k req/s, peak 3x. Proposals: (a) Redis session store, (b) stateless JWT in a cookie with 24 h life, (c) keep sticky sessions. Security requires "log out everywhere" and revocation within 1 minute. Cookies currently ~600 bytes.
questions.promptHtml: Which approach do you choose and why?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "JWT is stateless so it scales better," ignoring revocation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Session data size? Multi-region? Compliance on revocation? Mobile clients?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drain connections on deploy to reduce logouts.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Sessions in memory are lost on deploy; stickiness causes skew; JWT cannot be revoked without a denylist; Redis is a new dependency.
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure session size and read/write rate (5k req/s is trivial for Redis); failure drills; check cookie bytes per request.
  5. Root cause: State lives with the process; the fix is to move it out or sign it.
  6. Fix: Opaque session ID cookie (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax) with Redis (replicated, TTL sliding) giving instant revocation and tiny cookies; short-lived JWT access (5 min) plus refresh in Redis if stateless verification is required across services.
  7. Prevention: Redis failover test; fall back to re-login if Redis is down; session ID rotation on login; cap session size.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Pure long-lived JWT cannot meet revocation; Redis adds a network hop (~0.5 ms) and availability dependency; sticky sessions keep the scale problem.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Multi-region? -> Regional Redis with replication or global session service; accept re-login on failover.
  • Cookie bloat? -> Keep data server-side; every request carries the cookie.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team shipped 7-day JWTs, then needed an emergency denylist after a leak; they migrated to server sessions.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: JWT dogma.
  • Hire: Redis sessions with revocation reasoning.
  • Strong hire: hybrid short JWT, failure modes, cookie flags, numbers.

questions.contextHtml:
Users uploading 20-80 MB videos via POST /upload through nginx to a Java app sometimes get 413, sometimes a hang followed by 504 at exactly 60 s, and mobile users get connection resets halfway. Smaller files are fine. Config excerpts:

nginx: client_max_body_size 50m;  proxy_read_timeout 60s;  proxy_request_buffering on;
app: Tomcat maxPostSize default; upload handler writes to disk after reading all

Red herring: object storage is healthy.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose each symptom and redesign the upload path.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Raises limits and timeouts everywhere, leaving the architecture unchanged.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Max supported file size? Are mobile networks flaky? Is resumability required? Who validates content?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise client_max_body_size to the required cap, set proxy_request_buffering off for streaming, adjust timeouts to realistic bounds.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 413 from body-size limit (50 MB); 504 because the backend takes more than 60 s after buffering; resets from mobile network drops mid-upload with no resume; app buffering whole body in memory.
  4. How I'd verify each: nginx error log (client intended to send too large body), access log $request_time/$upstream_response_time, curl --limit-rate reproduction.
  5. Root cause: Large uploads travel through the app tier with fixed size and time limits; nginx buffers the full request before forwarding, then the app processes it slowly; any network blip restarts the transfer.
  6. Fix: Issue pre-signed URLs and upload directly to object storage with multipart/resumable upload (chunks of 5-8 MB), then notify the app; keep HTTP limits modest; return 202 with async processing.
  7. Prevention: Load tests with realistic slow clients, per-route limits, alerts on 413/504 rate, upload success-by-size metric.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Direct-to-storage needs CORS, token expiry and post-upload validation; not simply raising timeouts, which ties up workers and invites slowloris-style abuse.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why Expect: 100-continue? -> Lets the server reject before the body is sent.
  • Where to virus-scan? -> After upload in an async pipeline using the object-created event.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: moving uploads to pre-signed multipart URLs cut upload failures from 9% to under 1% and halved app-tier CPU.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises limits.
  • Hire: maps each symptom to a config cause.
  • Strong hire: direct-to-storage resumable design with trade-offs.
